name: Name
body: Battle Forge is a monthly series presenting a new Warmachine scenario in every installment. Battle Forge scenarios emphasize developing a narrative over the course of a game. They may be asymmetrical, uneven, and sometimes even wildly experimental. This is deliberate. The goal of Battle Forge is to create tools that you can use at the table to make your battles truly legendary! Modify this scenario as you need to in order to make it work for your army collections and the terrain you have available. Most important of all, have fun! And if you come up with any changes that make a scenario even better, let us know at feedback@privateerpress.com, so we can try it, too!

name: Name
body: Following are the key terms that will be repeated in many Battle Forge scenarios:

name: Name
body: Many scenarios utilize objectives. An objective can either be a terrain piece, a marker, or a zone designated on a terrain piece or on the map.

name: Name
body: Objective Markers are impassable terrain features and should be represented on the table with markers that are at least 20 mm in diameter. Unless otherwise specified, all Objective Markers used in a scenario should be the same size.

name: Name
body: To have more models in an area than your opponent does.

name: Name
body: An area or objective is contested if both players have models in the area or in scoring proximity to the objective at a time when scoring would take place. An area or objective is uncontested if only one player has models in the area or in scoring proximity to the objective when scoring would take place.

name: Name
body: The zone or the area of a terrain feature is held when a player occupies the area with two or more models, uncontested.

name: Name
body: An objective terrain piece or marker is secured when a player has two or more models within 1" of the objective, uncontested.

name: Name
body: Battle Forge victories can be determined by either achieving the goals of the scenario or through Victory Points, scored in a variety of ways throughout playing a scenario. Turn limits on scenarios put pressure on players to succeed within a set amount of turns, and Victory Points provide the means to determine victory when neither player has completed the primary objective of a scenario.

name: Name
body: In addition to its standard rules, each Battle Forge scenario has two random tables that add additional Victory Point-scoring opportunities for players that vary each time the scenario is played. Mission Modifiers add additional scoring opportunities based on the position of a player’s models on the table. Achievements add additional scoring opportunities based on a player’s actions taken on the battlefield. Players should roll a d6 to randomly determine Mission Modifiers and Achievements before the beginning of a game, or players can choose them at will if all players agree. It is recommended that only one Mission Modifier and one Achievement should be in effect during any match (unless you really want to get crazy).

name: Name
body: If a player makes an attack that destroys one or more friendly models, that player’s opponent gains 1 Victory Point. If a player makes an attack and destroys their own Leader model, that player immediately loses the match.

name: Name
body: In addition to objectives, Battle Forge scenarios will routinely draw on the following terrain elements. Dimensions provided are approximations, and you should feel free to substitute any terrain pieces you have available as necessary. Use the resources you have available to get close enough to maintain the spirit and intention of the scenario.

name: Name
body: An obstacle with an approximate footprint of 3/4" x 4". Barriers provide cover.

name: Name
body: Obstructions with an approximate footprint of 5" x 5".

name: Name
body: Forest areas with an approximate footprint of 5" in diameter.

name: Name
body: An obstacle with an approximate footprint of 2" x 2". Small obstacles provide cover.

name: Name
body: An elevated platform at least 1" above the table, such as a hill or terrace. Plateaus can possess multiple areas at different heights that models can be placed on, but the areas must be level to prevent models from falling over. If a model cannot be placed on a level area without risk of falling off, it cannot occupy that area. Models cannot be placed on slopes, and we recommend that plateau terrain with sloped surfaces not be used. Hill, Small—A plateau platform with a footprint approximately 6" in diameter and a level surface(s) at least 1" above the table that is large enough for five 30 mm models to be placed on. Hill, Large—A plateau with a footprint approximately 6" to 12" in diameter and a level surface(s) at least 1" above the table that is large enough for five 40 mm models to be placed on.

name: Name
body: An area of shallow water approximately 6" in diameter.

name: Name
body: An area of rubble approximately 6" in diameter.

name: Name
body: A 3" x 5" trench template.

name: Name
body: There’s a bounty of treasure to be found if you’re savvy enough to retrace the steps of him who stole it and shrewd enough to stay out of the crosshairs of him it was stolen from!

name: Name
body: "Hidden Treasure" is designed for 50- or 75-point forces.

name: Name
body: "Hidden Treasure" ends after six rounds.

name: Name
body: Players race to find a hidden treasure by following a series of clues to various points on the map. Only the player who secures a clue knows the location of the next clue, however, giving those practiced in the art of deception a possible edge over those who merely charge straight for the next objective.

name: Name
body:
Secure the treasure to win the match.
Score Victory Points by securing clues along the way.

name: Name
body: The map shown uses six small forests, three large ponds, two small hills, two large rubbles, four walls, three obstacles, and a building as well as six objective markers. But use whatever terrain you have available to create an interesting setup that blocks line of sight and makes the objectives somewhat challenging to reach so that models can’t simply beeline from one to the next. You will also need a cup that you cannot see through to cover a die during the match.

name: Name
body:
This scenario uses Execution Mode.
A series of three clues leads to the final treasure. A clue is obtained when a player begins their turn securing an objective that was determined to hold a clue.
The first clue is located in the central building. The first player to begin their turn securing the building rolls a d6 to determine which objective on the map holds the next clue. The result is not shared with their opponent, but the die should be placed under the cup mentioned in the Setup, with the result side up, so that it can be verified when the objective is secured.
If the result of a clue die role is an objective that has already been rolled, the rolling player shows the die to their opponent and rolls again.
Each time a player makes their opponent’s Leader Vulnerable, they can look at the die under the cup.
When a player who has not yet gained a clue begins their turn securing an objective, the player with a clue must reveal the die under the cup if the securing player has chosen the current objective to secure. The securing player then acquires the next clue by rolling the die to determine the next objective and concealing it under the cup.

name: Name
body:
The third time a clue is rolled for determines the final treasure objective.
When a player begins their turn securing the treasure objective, they win the match.
A player gains 1 Victory Point each time they get a clue.
A player gains 1 Victory Point each time they make their opponent’s Leader Vulnerable.

name: Name
body: Roll once on both the Mission Modifiers and Achievement tables.

name: Name
body: Roll a d3 to determine the Mission Modifier for this match: 1. Elementary— A player gains 1 Victory Point each time their Leader secures an objective to gain a clue. 2. Heavy Intel— All models securing an objective at the beginning of a player’s turn gain +2 DEF but must forfeit their Normal Movement or Action that turn. 3. Follow the Leader— If a player who has not yet gained a clue secures an objective from which their opponent just gained a clue, reveal the hidden die to them.

name: Name
body: Roll a d3 to determine the Achievement for this match. 1. Power Play— The first player to secure an objective after destroying opposing models that were securing it during the same turn gains 1 Victory Point. 2. Bingo— The first player to begin a turn securing any three objectives gains 1 Victory Point. 3. Devotion— The first player to share their clue with their opponent on the same turn they acquired it gains 1 Victory Point.

name: Name
body: Victory conditions are checked in the following order: Decisive Win: When a player begins their turn securing the third objective, or at the end of the second player’s sixth turn, the player securing the third objective wins the match. Point Advantage Win: At the end of any of the second player’s turns, if a player has 5 or more Victory Points than their opponent, they the match. Last Leader Win: At the end of any of the second player’s turns, a player with the last Leader model in play wins the match. Victory Point Win: If neither player has a Leader in play at the end of any of the second player’s turns, the player with the most Victory Points wins the match.
